concepts.def: Reduce, reuse, recycle, repair, rethink and refuse: a framework for cutting the environmental impact of products and consumption.
Evaluating a product's environmental impact at every stage: raw material extraction, manufacture, transport, use and end-of-life disposal.
The total greenhouse gas emissions associated with a product or activity, often dominated by energy used in manufacture and use.
A certification movement ensuring producers in developing countries receive fair prices and decent working conditions for their goods.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Implications Of Wider Issues — a core area of GCSE Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Implications Of Wider Issues brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Implications Of Wider Issues.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does a life cycle assessment evaluate?
options: A product's environmental impact across its whole life
How long a battery lasts on one charge
The profitability of a product line
The lifespan of the design team

mcqs.q: In the 6 Rs, what does 'refuse' mean?
options: Choosing not to buy or use unsustainable products or materials
Throwing waste into landfill
Returning faulty goods for a refund
Burning waste for energy

mcqs.q: What does Fairtrade certification primarily ensure?
options: Fair prices and conditions for producers
Zero packaging on products
The lowest possible retail price
Products are made by robots

mcqs.q: What is a product's carbon footprint?
options: The total greenhouse gas emissions associated with it
The floor space its factory occupies
The amount of carbon fibre it contains
The black marks it leaves on surfaces

mcqs.q: Are 'reuse' and 'recycle' the same thing in the 6 Rs?
options: Environmental impact is measured purely by the size of the packaging.
No — reuse means using an item again as it is or for a new purpose; recycling reprocesses the material into new products, which itself consumes energy.
Reuse means returning the product to the shop for resale.
Reusing and recycling are identical ways of dealing with waste.

mcqs.q: Does a product's environmental impact occur only when it is thrown away?
options: Products only harm the environment when they end up in landfill.
Environmental impact is measured purely by the size of the packaging.
No — life cycle assessment shows impacts at every stage: extraction, manufacture, transport, use and disposal; for appliances the use phase often dominates.
Reuse means returning the product to the shop for resale.

mcqs.q: Does Fairtrade certification mean a product is environmentally friendly?
options: Not necessarily — Fairtrade is primarily about fair prices and decent conditions for producers; it includes some standards but its core aim is social and economic.
Fairtrade means the product was manufactured in the United Kingdom.
A Fairtrade logo guarantees the product caused no environmental damage.
Environmental impact is measured purely by the size of the packaging.
